**Interpretation:** For $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n \geq 1$), I interpret $|\log(x)|$ as $|\log|x||$ where $|x|$ is the Euclidean norm.

## Proof

Using polar coordinates $x = r\omega$ with $r = |x| \in (0,\infty)$, $\omega \in S^{n-1}$, and $dx = r^{n-1}\,dr\,d\sigma(\omega)$:

$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |\log|x||^p\,dx = |S^{n-1}|\int_0^\infty |\log r|^p\,r^{n-1}\,dr$$

Split the radial integral at $r=1$:

$$\int_0^\infty |\log r|^p\,r^{n-1}\,dr = \underbrace{\int_0^1 |\log r|^p\,r^{n-1}\,dr}_{\text{Part 1}} + \underbrace{\int_1^\infty (\log r)^p\,r^{n-1}\,dr}_{\text{Part 2}}$$

### Part 2 (behavior at infinity) — diverges for all $p$

Substitute $r = e^t$, $dr = e^t\,dt$, $t \in (0,\infty)$:

$$\int_1^\infty (\log r)^p\,r^{n-1}\,dr = \int_0^\infty t^p\,e^{t(n-1)}\,e^t\,dt = \int_0^\infty t^p\,e^{nt}\,dt$$

For any $p \in \mathbb{R}$ and $n \geq 1$: as $t \to \infty$, the factor $e^{nt}$ grows exponentially while $t^p$ grows at most polynomially. For sufficiently large $T$, we have $t^p \geq e^{-nt/2}$ for all $t \geq T$ (since $t^p / e^{-nt/2} = t^p e^{nt/2} \to \infty$). Therefore:

$$\int_0^\infty t^p\,e^{nt}\,dt \geq \int_T^\infty e^{nt/2}\,dt = \frac{2}{n}e^{nT/2}\cdot\infty = \infty$$

**Part 2 diverges for every $p \in \mathbb{R}$.**

### Part 1 (behavior near origin) — for completeness

Substitute $r = e^{-t}$, $dr = -e^{-t}\,dt$, $t \in (0,\infty)$:

$$\int_0^1 |\log r|^p\,r^{n-1}\,dr = \int_0^\infty t^p\,e^{-nt}\,dt$$

- Near $t=0$: $t^p$ is integrable iff $p > -1$.
- Near $t=\infty$: $e^{-nt}$ ensures convergence for all $p$.

So Part 1 converges iff $p > -1$.

### Conclusion

Since Part 2 diverges for all $p \in \mathbb{R}$, the full integral over $\mathbb{R}^n$ diverges for all $p \in \mathbb{R}$, regardless of the behavior of Part 1.

**The integral $\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |\log|x||^p\,dx$ diverges for every $p \in \mathbb{R}$.** There is no value of $p$ for which it converges.

*Remark:* If the domain were restricted to the unit ball $B(0,1)$, only Part 1 would matter, and the integral would converge if and only if $p > -1$. The divergence at infinity over all of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is what eliminates every $p$.
